utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On behalf of the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Belinda Pidwell, Selma Sakic, and our Case Manager, Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Claire Plumb appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I requested to raise a couple of procedural matters before we brought the witness in. First of all, Ms. Pidwell has a couple of matters to address concerning scheduling and witnesses, and then I wanted to raise something concerning the exhibits we've been talking about with the witness that is returning this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. There are three matters I wish to address you on just at this stage, housekeeping matters. Firstly, your ruling last night in relation to ST-181 confused me slightly because I had already made the arrangements for that witness to come and testify and be re-called in that first week of January. And when we went back and checked the transcript, it appears that you had already directed us to do that on the 27th of November. So we had taken that as your ruling that we were directed to re-call that witness, ST-181, and have him called in January together with the one witness that we are coordinating with another team on, and our expert, Mr. Brown. I'm thinking, Your Honours, that maybe the confusion stems from the fact there is another motion by the Defence to re-call another witness, ST-191. And that still requires a ruling. You may recall Ms. Korner addressed you orally on that last week on the 30th of November, and we're waiting on a ruling on that witness, ST-191, to -- to know whether we need to bring him in addition to those three witnesses that we're required to bring in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I am aware that we have the ruling on 191 outstanding. But to the extent that we may have spoken inconsistently, Ms. Pidwell, I thank you for drawing it to our attention, and we will clarify what our position is with respect to the time when 181 should be re-called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, one question now. You say that you looked in the transcript of the 27th of November, and I don't seem to have a transcript on the 27th of November. Is that right, 27th?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's the 26th, Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I have it here in front of me. It's when Your Honours were directing us in relation to whether we could defer one adjudicated fact witness to January. And your ruling in respect of that witness also included on order -- what we understood to be an order in respect of ST-181. It's 17 -- T17910 on the 26th of November. And Your Honours concluded: We leave it to the Prosecution to determine in which order to call these witnesses, but the decision of the Chamber is that they -- these three must be completed by the week ending 17th -- or commencing 17th of January, 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You had two other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. The next is in relation to the witness who will follow the witness who is currently testifying; ST-065. He has protective measures of a pseudonym, and we have now become aware that his previous protective measures granted in the previous case were augmented on appeal and he, in fact, had -- was granted face distortion as well, after the -- after his testimony, so his testimony was revised. We sent a copy of that decision to the Trial Chamber last -- Legal Officers last night, and we're simply asking for confirmation that his previous protective measures will be confirmed by this Trial Chamber as well. As is he testifying next, he has some concerns, and we would like to be in a position to advise him as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we will deal with that in the course of today. Your third matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: My third matter, Your Honour, is in respect of ST-008. He is the witness who was due to testify last week but has been ill. We have -- the latest update from the hospital and through VWS is that he will be in a position to testify next week. So we are just giving an early indication that we will -- we are hoping to bring him on Monday if the witnesses for this week finish as scheduled, and that may mean that the Status Conference which the Registry are arranging may have to take place on Tuesday instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, it would -- the alternative was Wednesday, because I have a commitment on Tuesday. The -- today is Wednesday, so we would see your proposal in your usual Thursday list tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And if I may take a little bit of your time before the witness comes in to speak to the issue of the colour scans versus the black and white scans of the Mladic notebooks that have been MFI'd so far. And I direct your attention to page 18272, line 21, where Judge Delvoie asked a question of Mr. O'Sullivan whether his objection was that "the scans of all these different notebooks, there is a discrepancy in all the scan -- in the scans of ... these notebooks; right?" And Mr. O'Sullivan said: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE INQUIRED
utterances.text: "Can you give us an idea about what the nature is of the discrepancy?" And Mr. O'Sullivan said: "That might be best left for me to explore with the witness." In light of that, Your Honour - and I'm not attempting to testify, I'm just indicating something that I think you can see for yourself if you do a comparison - I took a look at tab 4, which has now been marked as Exhibit P1753 and P1754 for -- marked for identification, to compare the colour scan versus the black and white scan. It appears that there is no substantial difference in terms of the issue of authenticity with regard to the handwriting in those two scans. It appears the differences are other than the fact that one is in colour and one is black and white, and they have different ERNs in different places on the pages, obviously. The cover page was not scanned in the black and white scan. But the cover page is in the colour scan. The black and white scans were done in landscape format, so there are two diary pages per document. The colour scans are in portrait format, so there's one page of diary per one page of document. There, also, at the page following printed page number 400 in the notebook in the black and white scan there is a blank page. In the colour, that page was not scanned. I see no other differences in the two, and in the Prosecution's view, that is not a reason to not admit the colour scans at this point. I've seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I -- if I see where you're going, Mr. Hannis, our reasoning was - and to the extent that we may not have said it when we gave our ruling yesterday, I would indicate it now - that the exercise that you have just indicated you have performed in terms of that one exhibit would be done by you in respect of -- of all of the relevant exhibits. And that an oral application would be made when you would have -- when you would have completed this exercise. So the example that you have just given is the -- the result of that analysis and what I anticipate your application is going to be in respect of that exhibit is what we expect that we will hear when you would have -- when I "you," I mean the Office of the Prosecution, would have completed the exercise in respect of all of these parallel exhibits. And it's something that can be disposed of barring any startling discrepancies disposed of orally quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I guess it's my natural Prosecutor's anxiety being the one who bears the burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt and wanting to be sure that these, in the Prosecution's view, very important documents are going to be received in evidence. And I don't particularly care whether it's black and white or colour; we just thought the colour was more near to the original. Now, from what I hear you're saying and from Judge Harhoff said yesterday when he suggested that maybe the easy way around this was for me just to tender the black and white, and I thought about that last night and I thought, Well, yes, in a way this is what we do sometimes with documents where we may have a map or a photograph or a regular type-written document that the one we have in e-court is of pour quality for some reason - there wasn't enough toner in the printing machine when it was copied or it's hard to read or sometimes because there's a translation question - we then seek, later, to replace that one with a better quality document, a better copy of the photograph or an improved translation. So in effect, I guess I could ask that you admit the black and white versions now and then later on submit the colour versions once we've done that. Then I would have the comfort of knowing that when I'm done with this witness, those documents are in and I don't worry about having to try to apply to you to bring him back and get him in to tidy up something that he could tidy up while we still have the time before the 21st of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I would remind you - and this is something I do recall saying yesterday - that in essence there is no question about the admissibility of -- of the -- of the documents. So your apprehension about the possibility of having to recall the witness does not arise. The nature -- even if the objection of the Defence was to the admissibility of the content of the documents, which I didn't understand it to be, the Chamber -- the view of the Chamber was that the -- what the documents were about, the essence of the documents, was admissible; and they were given the parallel exhibit numbers because of this apparent - and I underline apparent - discrepancy between the two scanned versions. So the -- your invitation to us now to enter -- to -- to lift the -- the MFI clarification in respect of, say, the black and white versions with a view to the possibility of the -- their being substituted to the colour versions is, I would suggest, an unnecessary exercise, because, as I explained earlier, we expect that when you would have performed the examination, as is necessary, you would come back and tell us that we have done this and there's no discrepancy and the colour one should go in, or -- or, on the other hand, the black and white one should go in. So I don't know that we need take this any further at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. You've put my mind more at ease, and I'm ready to call the witness in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way in, Mr. Hannis, I would remind you that the three hours that you have been given in terms of your examination-in-chief with this witness, that what this witness has been called to testify to is the authenticity of the entries in the diary and therefore it isn't necessary for you to explore the incidents in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm not trying to do that at any length. Sometimes only to the extent that I think it does go to the basis of his opinion about why these particular documents are authenticate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, good afternoon to you. Before Mr. Hannis resumes his examination-in-chief, I would remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Welcome back, General. I just wanted to follow up a couple things regarding your knowledge about General Mladic's handwriting. You told us yesterday about the position you held and how you worked with him, and you had indicated that every day when you were in a meeting together with him you saw him writing in his work book, and you mentioned that whenever you were with him during any of the 1687 days that the Main Staff existed he was writing something. But I guess it's not clear from that, how often were you in meetings with him during those 1687 days? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was at the Main Staff, we had regular meetings, staff meetings, every morning and every evening. In the morning, we would set the task for the army during the day, and in the evening we would summarize and set tasks for the following day. Whenever we were together, Mladic made notes in his notebooks. Of course, I didn't stand behind him to watch what he was writing, but I did look upon from the side, because we usually sat next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how often did you have those meetings during the years you worked for him? Are we talking about a dozen times? Or hundreds of times? A thousand times?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over a thousand times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition to seeing him writing in his work book, did you see other examples of his handwriting? For example, did he give you notes asking for information, or assigning tasks, things like that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes when we were together at a meeting, he would pass slips to me when he wanted an explanation or wanted my opinion. And in order not to interrupt the others, he would pass me a slip of paper and I would answer him on that slip if I couldn't answer verbally. Most time you couldn't. And I said yesterday that we shared an office to save space; that was one reason. And the other was that Mladic was usually absent when I was there and the other way around. One of us was usually on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to the writing in the notebooks, did you occasions when other persons may have written in General Mladic's notebook? And, if so, can you explain how that happened.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that. But reviewing the notebooks these last few days, I saw that there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he ever show you what he was writing in the notebook during a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you something because of what you said yesterday. In looking at the first notebook with an entry from the 31st of December, 1991, you commented about General Mladic's particular style. This is at page 18249. Is that another means by which you have come to conclude that the writings in these notebooks are from General Mladic? Not just the handwriting but also the manner of expression.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the proofing, I said to you, and I repeated it yesterday, that after 14 years I recognised Mladic's handwriting based on the fact that he noted down what I was saying, but the other participants too, but primarily -- or on the basis of what I said. This is how I was able to recognise Mladic's handwriting. That's the most important reason, not because after 14 years I could recognise somebody's hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen the colour scan of tab 4. I think it's been marked as Exhibit 1753, MFI. And I'd like to start by showing the General the B/C/S page that is ERN J000-2807.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, near the middle of the page there is a box of text, and I want to ask you about the words written immediately above the box when you have it on your screen. Can you read us those two words?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this "my proposal," or which other two words could you mean? There is something in a box, but above that there are two words: "my suggestion" or "my proposal."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is there anything unusual about that to your mind, the way it's written?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is unusual how he phrased it. Yesterday in the text, we also saw two words, "nastup [phoen] moj," whereas grammatically -- it would be grammatically correct to have the inversion, "moj nastup" or "moj predlog," and not "predlog moj" as it says here. That's how he -- how he phrased it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever known anyone else to write it that way, with the word "moj" coming second in a phrase like that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. But I didn't have the opportunity to read other people's handwriting either. The logic could be the following: The proposal should have been made by the Chief of Staff or some of his collaborators, but since that -- since there was no such proposal then after the word "predlog," proposal, he put "moj" to indicate that it was his rather than somebody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page -- and the last four digits in the B/C/S ERN are 2878.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And if you could look at this one. The last sentence in the first paragraph. Do you see the last three words there? And can you tell us what they say in B/C/S and if there's anything unusual about the word order of that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which one you mean. You mean the first paragraph; right? There is a lieutenant-colonel contributing there, named Tosic. "I came back for the combat mission. I have two years before retirement. I am here in the capacity of Captain 1st Class. Once this is over, I want it to be clear where I came from. Response of mine." Again the inversion. Response of mine, we'll see about that. That's Mladic telling him we'll see about that. But instead of saying "my response" or "my reply," he phrases it in the following way: "Response of mine," or "reply of mine."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That all I wanted to show you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, I would like to go to 65 ter number 3582 -- I'm sorry, 3585.2. This is tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a -- this is a notebook that has entries for the period from 30 September until 4 October 1992. And I would like to begin by showing you an entry on page 12 of the English. It's page 22 of the B/C/S. This appears to be regarding a meeting on the 3rd of October of the corps of the General Staff of the VRS. Your name is among those present. Do you recognise the handwriting on this page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if you answered whose writing it was, it wasn't recorded. Could you tell us whose writing you recognise it as?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall attending such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was probably there, since he recorded my name as being there. Mladic; Milovanovic; Gvero; Djukic [as interpreted]; Tolimir; and Colonel Ilic, my deputy. This is a meeting of the inner circle of the Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the following page in B/C/S and keep the same page of the English up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to show you the next page in this notebook, and you'll see your name listed. Could you have a quick read of that and see if that helps you recall what this particular meeting was about. And tell us if you recall being there and speaking at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it out loud or just to myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can just read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I would like to tender 3585.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We object, Your Honour. The witness has looked at these two pages but there's no evidence that he's looked at this notebook before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, this is one of the five that this witness saw in Banja Luka in July 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no evidence from this witness that he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is in the witness statement of this witness that was provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, General, have you seen this notebook before? Have you had the chance to go through it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer whether I've ever seen this text. I did look at some of my texts and based on that I concluded that the handwriting was General Mladic's. I see no reason to not identify this as one of those texts that I recognised or identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that, General. But the point that is raised by the Defence is that your testimony to the authenticity may go only to the pages that you have looked at, and, hence, the question is whether, at some earlier point, you actually did have the chance to flip through this particular notebook and ascertain that all the pages in it were of the same handwriting. And that's fair enough. If do you not recall that you've seen it, then say so. But if you do recall -- or if you have been through them all, actually, then we would like to hear your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said yesterday, I've looked at a total of 23 notebook: five back in Banja Luka and 18 here. I have not read through each of them. That would have required far more time. But I did go through some notes that concerned me personally. I have read at least one from each of the notebooks. That led me to a conclusion that the notebooks were complete in as far as they were Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've now heard twice now, I think, that there was a meeting with the General and investigators from the OTP in July 2009 at Banja Luka. I wonder if we could be provided with a statement that may have been taken by the Prosecutor when apparently five books were shown to the General. We've received no such statement from -- by way of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that that was an audiotaped interview, and the audiotape has been disclosed to the Defence. The witness statement that reflects that the General reviewed 23 notebooks in total, including five in Banja Luka in the summer -- in July 2009, is a 65 ter document number 9141, and that also has been disclosed to the Defence. Now, we have proposed this witness as a 92 ter, or a 92 bis. All these documents could have been submitted. But now he's here. I have limited time to try to go through this with him. If it's really necessary, we can do that. I would propose to add 9141 -- well, I would propose now to be allowed to introduce 9141 and submit it into evidence concerning the five ERN ranges that were looked at the by the General in July 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the view of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution has sufficiently established the admissibility of this document. It may be admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1762, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would now like to move to 65 ter 3586. This is a notebook covering the period from 5 October 1992 to 27 December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment before we go on. Is this -- do we have a black and colour problem here again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. This one is just black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by "this one," I mean the one that we were just looked at that has been given the number P1762. But the one coming is one that has both colour and black and white, that's 3586, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General I would like to start off by showing you page number 111 in e-court in the B/C/S. And that's page 95 in the English. Do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this appears to be a recording of events on the 31st of October at a meeting of the 21st Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would note that Exhibit P179.15 in evidence are the minutes of that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know that General Mladic regularly attended Assembly sessions in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part he would be there. Gvero would be there. And normally Colonel Tolimir as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you learn from him about what transpired at those Assembly sessions he attended in any meeting of your Main Staff or General Staff after such sessions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from him. If there was any information to be conveyed to the Main Staff, that was normally done by General Gvero, his assistant for morale, religious, and legal issues. I see here that the agenda contains a total of 81 items. I don't think anyone would have been able to reproduce each and every one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Do you recall General Gvero advising the Staff of the results or summarizing what took place at Assembly sessions attended by General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I told you what the general principle was. Gvero would convey any information to the Main Staff and subordinate units. Anything that concerned any major issues that were discussed at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we go to page 297 of the B/C/S and page 320 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting on this page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is General Mladic's handwriting. Combined in red and in black pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we see a reference to the 23rd Session of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate that 65 ter 1749 is a transcript of the 23rd Assembly Session on the 17th of December, 1992. That is currently on the list of our bar table motion as one of the documents we'd like to tender. I propose to tender at this time, but if you prefer to deal with it as part of the bar table motion, that's fine with me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's a question of our preference, Mr. Hannis. We have a motion, we have a live motion in terms of the bar table -- the contents of the bar table motion and we have your application now. Is it your application that this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you say this is, again, a colour, black and white --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. But I was also moving to tender the 65 ter number of the Assembly session at the moment. That's what's the subject of the bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see. Which is a companion document to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm trying to introduce that document to corroborate what's in the diary, and I'm trying to introduce the diary to corroborate the 65 ter document, that is, the minutes of the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we -- your use of the word "corroboration" in our view adds an unnecessary complication insofar as whereas that may be an argument that the Prosecution may wish to advance when all of the evidence is in, confining ourselves to what this witness's testimony is about, that is, the authenticity of the notebooks we would prefer not to consider the companion documents as a part of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... all right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And therefore the order is limited to this document which is admitted and marked. And as I said, these would be parallel exhibits as we would have been following from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, therefore, the colour document will become Exhibit P1763; and the black and white version will become P1764, both marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to go to tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a handwritten work book covering -- actually, it's an excerpt from a handwritten notebook covering the period between 29 January 1993 and 31 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I have page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S. Your Honours may recall that we've sought to admit the entire notebooks for 1992. For 1993 we ask permission to admit only certain excerpts. So from these notebooks I'm only showing excerpts. And this first one -- yes, the 65 ter number is 3587.1. It's tab 22 on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, in a minute I hope to you show you an excerpt from that notebook from a meeting on the 6th of February, 1993. Do you see that, General? It's Saturday, 6 February, 1993, in Doboj, a meeting with political structures. Do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I need to draw your attention that the sound I'm receiving is not particularly clear in my headset. Secondly, this is General Mladic 's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll have somebody take a look at your headset.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear him well, but not the interpreters. All right. I can hear them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for letting us know, and please do advise if the problem re-occurs.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably something to do with my profession, because I used to drive a tank back in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Some similarities, I suppose. General, do you know anything about this meeting in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a political meeting, and I didn't do politics during the war. Not because I refused to but because it wasn't in my job description. My job description was about waging war, not politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this excerpt. It is from the notebook whose range you see on my list of documents to use with this defendant [sic] and that is item number 3 among the five exhibits looked at in July of 2009 in 65 ter 9141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't recall the witness confirming that he recognised the handwriting. Oh, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He did say that at the same time he was advising us about the problem with the headphones. And in light of that, I would ask to tender this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, could you remind me, Mr. Hannis, as to the evidential purpose of tendering this entry from 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this reference makes -- this entry makes reference to permission from Stanisic to form the Red Berets in Ozren and goes on to say that Mico wrote an order for Bozovic to form a special unit at the CSB in Doboj. We've heard other evidence in this case about Red Berets operating in the area of Doboj, we have evidence in this case that Mico Stanisic was no longer the minister in February of 1993, but we say this goes to the issue of knowledge, of failure to punish, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, again, is this -- are there two versions of this or just the black and -- monochromatic version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is one -- this is one of the monochromes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1765, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have just a moment. Thank you. Next, I'd like to turn to tab 24, which is 65 ter number 3588. And this is another notebook from 1993 covering the period from 2 April to 24 October, and we have a few excerpts from this. I'd like to start first by showing the witness page 4 of English and page -- well, I'm sorry, we have renumbered it in light of the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could have page 20 of the English, and I think it's 24 of the -- and 20 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is about the meeting of the 26th Session of the Assembly on the 2nd/3rd of April in Bileca. Do you recognise the handwriting on this page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's General Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think I would like to do all the excerpts from this particular book at one time and then move them in as one. Page 1 of the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object. This is 1993, minutes of an Assembly meeting. What relevance does that have in relation to the period covered by the indictment, which is 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, that was the question I had asked in respect of the last item which was admitted. And -- well, I'm not going to put words in Mr. Hannis's mouth, but what is your reply, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, let me find the reference. Are we talking about the one that's on the screen now, or the previous one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, the one that's on the screen now. And you indicated that there are a number -- I don't know how many more of these there are. You indicated that you would seek to admit them as a bundle. Perhaps not as a bundle but together, I think, was what you had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a -- this particular excerpt involves a meeting with Red Cross representatives. There's a discussion of camps and prisoners of war. There's a reference to the number of prisoners released from Manjaca and Trnopolje numbering more than five thousand. There's some prisoners of war still being visited. And they talk about persons still being detained in Batkovic, et cetera. So we think it's relevant to the issue of the detentions, the claims that all camps had been closed and all civilians released. So it goes to knowledge and the acts of cruel treatment that are alleged in the indictment. And it was admitted by -- we were allowed to add it to our 65 ter list when we -- when we made the submission to -- to Your Honours. It's by an order dated 17th of September, 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, that's step one. The addition to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. But I trust, Your Honours, the reason you allowed us to add it to the list was because we initially persuaded you that it was relevant and probative, even though it was outside the time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Although Mr. Krgovic didn't expand his objection the way I'm going to pose this question to you now, the admissibility of documents outside of the period covered by the indictment is -- it's well settled that it is permissible for certain purposes, but mustn't there come a point, Mr. Hannis, when we are being invited to admit documents which because they fall outside the relevant period of the indictment ought not to be admitted? The arguments of continuity and system and consistency apart, and against that background - as I said, I don't know how many of these documents you have; you indicated you have a number - mustn't each of them be considered separately for admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, that's how I would treat it. Each one should stand or fall on its own merits. But we do believe that it is relevant even though it's after the time-period. We have persuaded you in the past to admit some documents outside the time-period, for example, some Assembly sessions where there were discussions about what had been done during the time-period, how they did it, who they worked with, et cetera. And, as I said, this goes to an issue that's been contested in this case about the number of people that were at those camps and whether they were camps, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So this one may be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1766, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next one I have is for the 27th of May, 1993. And page number -- page number 8 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a -- about a meeting in Banja Luka on the 27th of May, 1993. Do you recognise the handwriting on this page? If so, who is it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It's the handwriting of General Mladic. He held a meeting with officers from the 1st Krajina Corps and the air force and anti-aircraft defence in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this is a little longer excerpt. In fairness, I think we need to go forward three pages in both the English and B/C/S to show you the part that we suggest is most probative, even though it's outside the time-period. General, you recognise the handwriting on this page as well?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It's the same handwriting. It's General Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The name at the bottom that's underlined above item number 1, Colonel Bogojevic. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. He was the chief of the intelligence service in the 1st Krajina Corps command. He was an intelligence man in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And my English translation says that he's reporting that Simo Drljaca has arrived. He was sent by the minister of the RS, and he came about the Tomasica mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, same handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it carries on: near Prijedor where earlier they buried around 5.000 Muslims, Drljaca came to leave this with us, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, you will see what this relates to from 1992, and we think it's highly relevant and probative, and I would tender this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P1767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more from this diary. And it's page 15 of both the English and the B/C/S. It's an excerpt from the 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you recognise the handwriting on this page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It's the handwriting of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This is about the 34th Session of the Assembly in Banja Luka on the 29th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page. I'm sorry, could we go two pages in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, in General Mladic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's General Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, among other items on this page is a discussion by Tomo Kovac about tension between the army and the police about -- about golfs coming out of the TAS factory in June of 1992. Mico Stanisic is noted as speaking about the golfs. And we would move to tender this one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, here we're well into 1993, into September. What --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- we think it goes, again, to knowledge and failure to punish. We think -- and there has been evidence in this case about police being involved in the theft of those golfs. Evidence about those golfs being taken to Serbia and sold in order to buy equipment for the police. And therefore this continuing discussion about it and Mr. Stanisic's involvement in it we think make it relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think, I believe, the simply question is where in the indictment are we talking about Golf cars?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're talking about the failure to punish policemen. We're talking about a joint criminal enterprise. We're talking about the means to furnish and equip and supply those who committed the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, as Their Honours pointed out, we're in September 1993. Mr. Stanisic is not the minister. Whether or not this accurately reflects what was said is also not established. We're outside the time-frame of the indictment. Mr. Stanisic is not the minister of the interior at this point. And the matters on the surface don't appear to relate to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber does not accept that this item should be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As it is clearly outside of the period covered by the indictment and there is no obvious connection between the contents and the -- what it concerns and the matters charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Let me ... let me consult for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like text to turn to tab 28. This is 65 ter number 3592.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just a technicality. This last excerpt came from which notebook? Notebook under tab number ... which tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, all those excerpts -- all those excerpts from 1993 between April 2nd and September 29th, or whatever that last one we looked at, were from tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted as 1766; right? 1766.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I had proposed to have multiple excerpts admitted as one, but then I think we started marking them -- considering them individually. So I think we need to give them separate 65 ters and -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, because this way we only have one -- Madam Registrar, we only have one number, haven't we? Yes. So we can't distinguish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. So that's my request, that we can mark the excerpts as 3588.1, 2, 3, and 4, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And 4 being not admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And 4 being not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's the solution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this last one if we could go to -- well, first of all, if we could look at the cover page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] General, you mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that later on in the war when you ran out of JNA work books that General Mladic, and I guess the rest of you, started using other kinds of notebooks that you could find from -- from any source to write in your daily entries about your work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mladic received a large quantity of notebooks such as this one from Sogovic [phoen], the director of the petroleum industry of Serbia, such as this one, and I received some from the print shop in Drvar. Everybody tried to find what they can. We didn't have the standard JNA notebooks any longer, so we made our entries in other notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go to page -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In B/C/S, I need the ERN 0649-0552. And in English it's page number -- page 224 in English and 227 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's General Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could continue to the next page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, same question: Whose handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's the handwriting of General Mladic, except he switched pens towards the end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go back one page in both the B/C/S and the English, we'll see that this is an about a meeting that occurred on the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did you know about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. At that time I was defending us from Operation Storm in the general area of Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the military Operation Storm. I'm not referring to a storm as in relating to the weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. I'd like to show you a video, briefly, that is of this 11 July 1995 meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, on the face of it, how is a meeting in July of 1995 relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not trying to admit this entry for its content. This is only on the issue of the authenticity of the notebooks. This is similar to the video I showed of the Assembly session in Banja Luka in May 1992. I think I have a better connection of tying the notebook in the video to the notebook from which the General has just identified the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But the testimony of this witness has been led to establish the authenticity of those entries in the notebook on which you are seeking to rely. And we have painstakingly, from yesterday, gone through a series of entries. So, in other words, each of the entries on which you are relying you led evidence to establish the -- its authenticity. If by the time we get to 1995 you can't be relying on what it's about, what is the purpose of going through the exercise and establishing the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, it goes back to my, I guess, initial anxiety and feeling like I needed to provide you belt and suspenders. But if what I'm hearing you say is that I don't need to do this, then I won't. I would make a statement, as proffered evidence: What I propose to show was, you've seen this notebook, you've seen an entry for a meeting on the 11th of July, the witness has identified the handwriting of being of General Mladic, the video shows General Mladic at that meeting with those persons named, and you can see on the video an open notebook which appears to have the same kind of watermarks on it, et cetera. And I'm trying to make that link. I think you're telling me I don't need to do that. And if that's the case, it's almost time for the break and -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's -- it's not for the Bench to tell you how to run your case, Mr. Hannis. The only question I have is in terms of the rules of relevance, which is fundamental to every trial, and in a criminal matter relevance being formed by the indictment, or being based on the indictment, how is this, on the face of it, at all relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in light of the Defence's continuing challenge to the authenticity of these notebooks, our position is that part of the evidence that establishes the authenticity of the notebooks include things you haven't heard yet but which you would hear from Investigator Tomasz Blaszczyk and/or Investigator Ellen Gallagher about the circumstances in which these were found in a group together behind a closed wall in the house of the General's wife. All those kind of things suggest that all of these were made by one person and that person was Ratko Mladic; and, therefore, if I can show conclusively that the 1995 notebook is from Ratko Mladic, then I bolster my argument that say that all the rest are. That's the purpose of why I'm trying to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we take your point that it's time for the break. We will rule on this when we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way in, we have considered the application to admit the last document that the Prosecution had on the screen. In our view that it is -- that it ought not to be admitted because it doesn't -- it is irrelevant as not advancing the issues in respect of which this witness was called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I make one further application to you. What I had proposed to show was the video in which at a certain point you can hear some of the people in the video speaking. You can see briefly General Mladic writing in a notebook that he has in front of him. It's the Prosecution's position that if you look at the original notebook can you see that there this is an entry about the very subject that was spoken about by the person in the video and that the pages appear to have the same kind of design or water mark, if you will, on the top of the pages that are in the notebook. And in connection with that, Your Honour, I have handed, during the break, to the Registry Officer the original notebook that is reflecting that meeting in July of 1995, and I have proposed to just hand it up as a demonstrative exhibit for Your Honours to see the size and texture, et cetera, of the notebook and also perhaps to show it to the witness to see if he can confirm if indeed that original has the General's handwriting. But I don't want to offer that book into evidence because it needs to go back to the evidence unit to -- we're trying to retain strict control of all those originals. Also, I need to point out it is not the same you heard -- this is from a private supplier; this is not the JNA notebooks that were used earlier in the war, because they ran out of those. We have some of those in the evidence unit as well, but those are being preserved for the moment for the possibility of forensic testing for DNA in the event that the person whose DNA might be on it shows up sometime in the near future. And I'm not permitted at the moment to bring that in and show you. But, by your leave, if you -- your ruling is that you don't want to see the video, then I would simply ask if we can hand that notebook to the witness and ask him if he recognises it and if he recognises the handwriting at the tabbed entry on 11 July and then I'll stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the reasons that we indicated earlier, Mr. Hannis, the -- there's no point in showing the video. In terms of what you propose to do in terms of this notebook, the -- you could ask your question and we see where it goes. I may be missing something, but it seems to me that the problem in terms of this item is that it is affected by the same vice as the excerpt and the video. But proceed and we'll see where you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I -- I see that you've seen it, and that kind of satisfies the demonstrative purpose for which I wanted to produce it, so I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you, Mr. -- if I seem tentative it is because I am not sure what we have seen. It seems to be unusual for an item to be laid over to the Bench without it being properly exhibited. But it has happened, and I don't know -- we'll see, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one prior experience in this Tribunal; that in the Milutinovic case we had a train log from the train station, we had the original, we had a man who helped keep it who came in and talked about it but requested that he be allowed to return the original to his place of employment because it was necessary. And with the agreement of all concerned, we allowed the original to be taken away because we had a copy and it was on the record of what we had done. And we were allowed to substitute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that practice. For instance, in my own experience elsewhere it would arise in the case of land documents, for instance, conveyances and that sort of thing, where the witness is allowed to take the original back and you treat the photocopy, or whatever have you, as the working exhibit. My query in this case is that - and I chose not to examine it myself - that the impression I had is that this wasn't the -- in any sense the original of what had been exhibited. It was the original of what had not been exhibited. That was the only query I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had shown him on the screen the entry for July 11th, which is tabbed in this book, and he did identify that handwriting as the handwriting of General Mladic. But I had -- when we had a discussion about -- I said I was not trying to offer that entry for the -- for the content of the July 11th but trying to connect it with the video which showed the General actually writing in a book and then trying to establish a link between what's shown in the video and this exact book. But it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But you -- you say you're through with your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in light of your rulings, I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I would like to present a hard copy of P1750 to the General. It's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- chart that he filled out. It would be easier for him to follow in hard copy, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: General, you're looking at a copy of Exhibit P1750, which is the form you completed on the 22nd of April, 2010. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on that day, you were at the office -- within the Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I testified in the latter half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, but during this meeting on the 22nd of April, the meeting you had with the Prosecutor took place here in The Hague in the Prosecutor's offices; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the so-called proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. And at the time, you were told by the Prosecutor that the documents you looked at were obtained from the Government of the Republic of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you were not told where the Government of Serbia had obtained those documents; am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't told, nor did I inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this document indicates that you looked at 18 documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat again: I reviewed five in Banja Luka and 18 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And the 18 that you looked at here, that all took place on the 22nd of April during that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not only on the 22nd. I signed this on the 22nd. The proofing with the OTP took two days. So I reviewed these in two days and only signed this paper on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at instruction number 1, you see you were asked to confirm whether the page range in column 2 is correct or not. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I was requested to write or -- the correct number where the numbers did not match, and that is what I did on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I see that you did not answer column 6, and you explained that you didn't do that because you did not have enough time to study the documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to assist me. Column 6 has a heading: "Personally acquainted with the event." It was unclear to me which event was -- is meant here. The seizure of the work books, the handling of the work books, or the events described in the work books.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I was simply referring to the handwritten note you made at the bottom of page 2 where you just said, I did not have time to study each document. Is that -- you wrote that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at -- on the second page -- well, yes, on the second page, you noted a discrepancy in the second column with the page range; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the page numbers. I was requested to correct that by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I see that you made the correction. You -- you wrote in that the last page was 3270.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that. Which page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It will be the second page for you. You see document number 6? It's the first entry on the second page, number 6. And column number 2, you wrote: "3270. You wrote the 270, you --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zero, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, if do you the mathematics, that document that you looked at appeared to have 73 pages. The information we have from the Prosecutor is that document should have 397 pages, based on the ERN. So on that day you looked at a document -- based on this form, you looked at a document that was 73 pages, not 397 pages. Does that seem right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to confirm or deny. I did what I was requested to do, but I did not count the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And if the page difference is between 397 and 73, I suppose it's fair to say that the document indicated on the list is different than the one you looked at. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible. If that was a standard JNA work book, then it had 400 pages. A few pages at the beginning are deducted where there's a calendar, internal notes, phone numbers, and so on; whereas, the blank pages start with page 13 and the last page that can be used is 399. Whereas, page 400 is reserved for certifying the work book.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we've seen your annotation. Entry number 8, you mark it -- there's a discrepancy there, apparently. You put the number 1 -- 2081. The "1" you included. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Entry number 9, there appears to be a discrepancy as well. You pencilled in "93." So it's 4493 instead of 4478. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But, sir, I now remember what this is about. I got this sheet which is a list of documents or work books. It was my task to compare the numbers stated here in this list with the numbers on the documents themselves. And if the numbers didn't match, and it was mostly the last digits that didn't, my task was to enter the correct number as indicated on the document. I don't understand that as counting pages. I understood that to mean that wherever the number on the -- in the work book doesn't match the number mentioned in the document, I was supposed to correct the numbers, and I did so on this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very well. I just want to confirm that I've understood your entries. But we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, you didn't ask to have this document on the screen, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it was P1750. I'm sorry. I assumed that -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yeah, but it's because I don't -- I can't follow. So that's why I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. I was focussed on the hard copy, and I didn't request it. I'm very sorry. P1750. We're on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think it's -- your explanations are quite clear. We understood that you were asked to put the actual pages or the numbers that you saw, and you did that. I just want to go through this document to confirm what you did. We just looked at document number 9. Document number 10, again, you noted a discrepancy. 1282, you corrected; you added "282." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which item number is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... number 10.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. 282.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Again, a discrepancy in document number 11. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I wrote a number 1 instead of whatever there was originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Document number 12, again.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote "3985," whereas, originally it read "4069."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There what purports to a 156-page document only has 72 pages. So it seems like a very different document that you looked at there, at number 12.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for the Prosecution to know. I don't know that. I didn't count the pages because that wasn't my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Document 15, you note a discrepancy. Instead of 77, it's 56. You pencilled in "56"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So that would be, instead of a 95-page document, a 74-page document. 17, again, you pencilled in "10." Do you --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know what there was originally, because I used a black pen and now the original numbers can no longer be made out.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And we can only base it on what the Prosecution has used in this trial, and they say it's 2003, but we'll see. And document 18, you have changed -- you have added a "1," "0931." And "111," becomes "1153."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So, in fact, this document appears to have more pages than what was indicated on the sheet. I believe it's correct that in the days following the 22nd of April, the Prosecutor came back to you to correct only one discrepancy in document number 3. They've showed you one more page and you confirmed that that page was missing. Do you recall that happening?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which document you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the Prosecution coming to you in the days following with one -- one page to say this -- this page should have been included in the documents they supplied you with? Do you recall that happening?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before or after my testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I would think prior to your testimony but after filling out the form in front of you. If you don't recall, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, but it's possible. It certainly can't have been after the testimony because I know that we bid each other farewell then and went our own separate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. So you don't recall the Prosecution reacting to the changes you made to this form?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think I spent two or three days with the Prosecution before the testimony, and I really don't know when I did what. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine, sir. If you don't recall, that's perfectly all right. In July 2009, apparently you were asked to look at five documents. You've talked about that. The five documents in July 2009 in Banja Luka. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you did not fill out any similar form in 2009 at that time. Am I correct in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in April 2010 - I'm talking about the second meeting - you were not shown those five documents again, were you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't. I don't think so. I reviewed 18 documents, as is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: As you sit here today, you would have no idea what the page range of those five documents that you saw in Banja Luka is, do you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But we discussed those work books even in August 2009, which is the following month.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I heard you say yesterday - I just want to confirm this and perhaps refresh your memory - at page 18338, regarding the five books in Banja Luka, you said: "I didn't read through them all, but I asked for permission to read those sections of the notebooks that referred to me." That's the way it was in Banja Luka, was it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it was in Banja Luka, and the purpose of that was to jog my memory also with regard to Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to change topics just for a moment. You explained to us yesterday that because of your -- or through your years in the JNA and the VRS as an officer, keeping a notebook was something that senior officers did. And is it correct that there was a certain protocol that was followed, in that the officer would insert his name and first name and rank or registry at the beginning of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the JNA, when you were issued the notebook which was done in an office, the one who received the notebook had to sign the log-book of issued notebooks. I saw one of Mladic's notebooks, I believe, from 1990 or 1991, which was entered. Once it was full, it had to be returned. Usually lower-ranking officers would return them. You said high-ranking officers, but all officers had work books, from squad commanders to army -- the army commander. But higher ranking officers wouldn't really return work books often because the NCO in charge of these matters wouldn't dare oppose them. So that the work books, the used work books, would mostly left with the higher-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Mladic, based on your experience with him in 1992 to 1995, during that period, did he enter his name and -- and first name and other information in his notebooks? Do you recall seeing that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. None of us wrote down our names for practical reasons. In case any of us were captured, the notebook too would be seized. The enemy's investigator or interrogator in that case would have had no trouble at all ascertaining the person's identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the second time in this courtroom, good afternoon, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We know each other. We had an opportunity to meet in the Popovic case and other times too. The last time around I took my time with you, quite some time. I will try to keep this brief for a change. I don't have so many questions for you, sir. General, sir, do you remember yesterday when you talked about the tactical groups and my learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you about the TG 3 commander and the TG 9 commander, Colonel Lisica - we're talking about Colonel Slavko Lisica; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I wasn't talking about TG 9; I was talking about TG 3 and Operations Group 9, OG 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the TG 3, and Colonel Lisica was first the commander of that group and then later he became the commander of OG 9; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. A tactical group is a provisional unit which is formed to carry out specific tasks over a specific period of time. In this case, the objective was to take Bosanski Brod. Once that was done, the group disbanded and Lisica was transferred to OG 9. Nevertheless, this OG as well is a temporary unit, but this one stayed the way it was throughout the war. It had the level, roughly speaking, of an infantry division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who preceded Colonel Lisica as head of the OG? It was Milivoj Simic, if I'm not mistake. Do you know about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to ask you is this: You said yesterday that Brod was liberated on the 7th of October, 1992. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I didn't use such terms as "liberated" or "occupied" during the actual war. The terms I used were such terms as "taken." It was, after all, a single state. It is impossible to liberate a town that is in one and the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is this: Do you know that Colonel Lisica became commander of OG 9 sometime in November 1992? Meaning sometime before the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Brod was taken and TG 3 was disbanded, Lisica took over as commander of OG 9. Or OG Doboj, as we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you wouldn't happen to know the date or the month, would you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first half of November. I can't give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I checked this information, too, and that's why I'm asking. So it was the first half the of November; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I remember is this: The now-General Lisica, at the time Colonel Lisica, and General Mladic in addition to have this relationship of subordination, one being superior to the other, were also friends on personal terms. When Mladic was about to appoint him commander of OG 9, Mladic called me, he phoned me, and ordered me to draw up an order or instructions to set up the 3rd Krajina Corps, to draw up a decree to set up the 3rd Krajina Corps. I asked him about the specific area of responsibility for that corps, and he said between Ucine region and Bosnia. Which led me to conclude that neither he nor Lisica knew much about geography, because the Bosnian region is next to Ucine and this was Central Bosnia. You couldn't possibly have a 3rd Krajina Corps in that area. If he wanted to promote Lisica to the rank of general, he should have ordered a restructuring effort for the whole of the VRS so that this officer could now become an alternative general-major. And that's how the whole thing ground to a halt. It was sometime in mid-November. I did not produce that decree.
