Three days later, Mladic tried to push me to work faster upon which I had to explain that this was impossible. We would have had more corps around than brigades had that become the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, thank you for this explanation. Just to go back to the log-books that your evidence focussed on. If I understand your evidence correctly, when you received the log-books with the purpose of checking whether the handwriting was Mladic's, at first sight could you not identify Mladic's handwriting. You had to look for entries in which your name was mentioned so that jogged your memory about the substance being discussed in the log-books. Wasn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the case. I identified Mladic's handwriting. Nevertheless, as I said yesterday and today a short while ago, the last time I actually saw Mladic while we were both working in the army, it was 14 years ago, 1996. I simply wanted to see for myself that this was, indeed, Mladic's handwriting, how -- by reading certain portions of those notebooks that were in relation to me. Which would have jogged my memory as to whether I actually said those words or not that I was recorded as saying. The first section or excerpt from these notebooks that I read was about the Main Staff meeting at Oskarin [phoen] on the 4th of August, 1995. That was still vivid in my memory. Why? Because I attended that meeting, and at that meeting I - meaning not Mladic or the General Staff - refused to carry out an order by the Supreme Command. Mladic asked me whether I was fully aware of my actions, and I said, yes, that indeed I was fully aware that I was potentially facing arrest or being court marshalled. I wasn't in favour of General Mladic being removed from his post at the war's end. Simply because there were no reasons for that. The reasons were of a purely political nature. I read every single word of my contribution at the meeting as it was recorded, and everything was consistent. Leading me to conclude that that was indeed Mladic's notebook. I do have to tell the Trial Chamber something else now that you started me talking about this, if I may put it that way. What I read at the time in Banja Luka seven days later appeared in "Slobodna Bosna" magazine. Nevertheless, it didn't say Milovanovic there, so the journalist had to explain who said what at the meeting. But I didn't check that at the time. And then it keeps saying a person named "N Sh." He didn't know who the person was. He thought those were initials for someone's name. And the next time Mr. Nicholls came, I showed him the article from "Slobodna Bosna" magazine and I wanted an explanation. The only person knowing about what I said at the time was me and an investigator whose name I can't remember and the interpreter who was there. Nevertheless, it's a fact that there were other things that occurred on that date that the papers got hold of, things that the interpreter didn't know of, things that I had never read myself. I never received a satisfactory explanation as to how this information cropped up in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your explanation, sir, in order to be 100 per cent certain that this was Mladic's handwriting and Mladic's diaries, you went through some of the substance. But did you not cross-reference that to perhaps another sample of Mladic's handwriting or a handwriting in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have any documents in my possession. None that I failed to hand over. I never had anything like that in my possession. Mladic never produced combat documents in handwriting. He would write something down in hand that would be sent through a teleprinter, typed up, and sent in that format to any of his subordinate units or whoever the document was addressed to. During my time working with him, I never saw a document that he wrote in hand. As soon as he wrote something down, he would immediately forward it to the person in charge of the encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What this means is the OTP never asked you to compare this diary to something that was in indisputably Mladic's handwriting; they just wanted you to quickly check it for authenticity; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Objection. It calls for speculation on his part to say what the OTP was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this that's precisely what I was asking. What was the task given to you by the OTP? To --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, could I have a ruling on my objection? It calls for speculation for this witness to say what the OTP was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's a problem with translation. I never said about what -- I asked what Prosecution did. Ask, not think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the -- I see nothing with -- objection about your question in substance, but perhaps it could be rephrased. You can ask a direct question; you're cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, what did the OTP want you to do specifically when they gave you these diaries to look at?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will keep it short and clear. They wanted me to identify the handwriting to say whether it was Mladic's or whose handwriting it was. Nevertheless, I came across Mladic's handwriting while meeting another OTP team a year or two earlier on headed by Mr. Mark Harmon. And this, too, occurred in Banja Luka. They gave me documents to look at that were signed by General Mladic. All sorts of different orders and what have you. We had some trouble -- or, rather, I had some trouble recognizing Mladic's initial, RM, standing for Ratko Mladic, simply because General Tolimir's initialling were quite alike, ZT, Zdravko Tolimir. Nevertheless, I did come across Mladic's initials whenever he signed combat orders which he had to sign by using his full name, Ratko Mladic. When the notebooks arrived, I was already getting into my stride, as it were, with Mladic's handwriting through the documents that I had looked at and through his signatures that I had seen. Or else he received a document from someone, the Supreme Command or perhaps one of the subordinate units. And then if you look at the heading of the documents, he would normally write there, "forward to the Chief of Staff." Or else he would write, "Chief of Staff, your opinion, your proposal, deal with this," or something to that effect. Therefore, there was a bit more text in these sentences that he wrote explaining the nature of the document. He would write that sort of thing down so the courier knew who he would bring the document to, to deal with it. Or else these were suggestions being made to his subordinate officers as to what exactly to do with those documents. It was a bit more text there than just initials or the signature. So I familiarised myself with Mladic's signatures as early as the 2nd of July, 2007, or thereabouts, which followed my appearance here. Because the first time I talked to Mark Harmon was here, after my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, sir. The interpreters are asking you to slow down because you're speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Mr. Mark Harmon asked to speak to me right after I appeared in court here. Nevertheless, I was physically unable to make that appointment. I wasn't able to put up with it physically. I was ill at the time. And we can spoke here for two hours. We agreed for him to go to Banja Luka. We did joke about that, too. He's two years younger than me. It was easier for him to take that flight and get here than it would have been for me. He eventually arrived on 2nd of July, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, for the purpose of the present trial, you looked through diaries. The OTP did not ask you to compare that to Mladic's other signatures, for example his signature on his ID or the -- the files used by the police to produce someone's ID or any other certified document, official document. You weren't asked to compare his signature to any of his other signatures and documents such as those, were you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OTP had no need to do that. They simply asked me to identify the handwriting. For my part, I made a suggestion to the OTP. I said we should use Mladic's signatures in combat documents available to the Tribunal and to use those to have them analysed by handwriting experts who would then confirm whether the handwriting in the notebooks was consistent with the handwriting seen in Mladic's official signatures, as it were. It wasn't that I was trying to be cautious for my own sake. I simply wanted to let the OTP know that Mladic's signature was more readily identifiable to me by the substance of the document itself as opposed to my memory of Mladic's handwriting dating back 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That is because, needless to say, you're no handwriting expert yourself. I won't call you a layman, but you're only talking based on your own experience and knowledge of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war I used the Latin script to sign my own combat document. After the war, I used the Cyrillic to sign documents. If someone forced me to sign a document in the Latin script, I don't think I'd be able to anymore, let's alone attempt to make a faithful copy of Mladic's handwriting from 14 years ago. That's why I advised the OTP to enlist the assistance of a handwriting expert to confirm the consistency between the handwriting in the diaries and the handwriting found in combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's all I had to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me follow up with that last question. In spite of the fact that you, sir, are not a handwriting expert, given your long acquaintance with General Mladic, the thousand times you were in meetings seeing him writing, your knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the entries that you've told us about in these notebooks, and having re-acquainted yourself with the events from that many years ago, are you or do you have any doubt that these notebooks that you've identified as containing the writing of General Mladic are, indeed, authentic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I told you during proofing that you can't measure anything by a thousand per cent. But I'm 1000 per cent certain this is Mladic's handwriting. What I said regarding the graphologist, the handwriting expert, I'm repeating now merely because I suspect that modern technology can do everything. You can falsify travel documents, you can falsify any document. However, since there's a vast amount of this material and it was made in a short period of time, I believe that during the 14 years since our ways with General Mladic officially parted is little time -- is not enough time to reproduce all these pages. You can take this any way you want. If the Court will accept, I can guarantee that this is Mladic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General, in the process of writing these notebooks, General Mladic or yourself or any -- any of your colleagues, does it happen that you write in two different books about entries -- about the same period? So that, for instance, you would have a notebook from January 1995 to September 1995 and another one from July 1995 to September 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I didn't understand you. You're asking me whether it's possible that one notebook is from and until, and the other one, again, is from and until. If that's what you're asking me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and, in part, overlapping. The beginning and the end of one notebook is within the range of dates from the other, which would suggest that you take notes simultaneously in two books during the same period.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I used to do. And looking at Mladic's diaries, I could tell that that's what he was doing as well. He even allowed somebody else to write entries in his notebook. All of us officers in the Staff, for example, I had a large notebook where I kept the log of the Staff, however, when I went to the front I couldn't carry that notebook with me so then I would carry a smaller one on me if I needed to writing is down. I would write things down while I stayed in the subordinated units. In the evening or when I returned, I would copy these entries in my regular notebook. So you would find the small notebook and the large notebook. On occasion, I might have forgotten to copy the entry. And if I didn't copy it, then it would stay in the small notebook and there would be a gap in the large notebook. I had a separate notebook that I kept and carried with me. It was a nicer one and I kept it in my better uniform. When I went to a meeting with the generals of the opposite side or with UNPROFOR, I carried this notebook with me and I made entries about these meetings. Sometimes I carried it to the meetings of the Supreme Command. Since I noticed that I didn't copy things regularly to the main notebook, I kept that notebook as well, and luckily I still have it. So it's possible that there would be overlaps in two notebooks of the same entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, General, you told us in the beginning of your statement, I remember now, about the small and the large notebooks. So that clarifies the doubt I had about how this went about. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, General Milovanovic, for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have a brief oral ruling to deliver. The Chamber recalls that the Appeals Chamber, when seized of the Stakic case on the 19th of January, 2007, augmented the protective measures previously granted to ST-065 which was a pseudonym. The Prosecution in that case had requested face distortion for the witness's prior testimony before the Trial Chamber or, in the alternative, that the trial testimony be placed under seal. The Appeals Chamber found that the Prosecution had established a rare likelihood of danger or risk to the witness's security which necessitated augmentation of the protective measures. For practical reasons, since the request related to video recordings of prior testimony, the Appeals Chamber granted the Prosecution's alternative request and placed the prior testimony under seal. The witness has renewed his request for face distortion. The Chamber grants this application, and, in doing so, takes note of the Appeals Chamber finding regarding the security situation of the witness. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd rather like to tell the witness before he comes into court, so I'd ask Your Honours to take the adjournment now, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday Judge Delvoie asked me if I would have any submissions to make following the testimony of this witness. I'm prepared to make those submissions. When it pleases you. Either now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, now, if you would, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, our position is the following: We say that on the basis of Rule 95 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence these documents should be excluded from evidence. Rule 95 states that no evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast doubt, cast substantial doubts on its reliability or its admission as antithetical to or would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. What do we know about these documents? First we have a set of colour-scanned documents beginning the ERN range J000. Those are in the B/C/S language or perhaps in this case the Serbian language, handwritten Cyrillic. We have a set of black and white-scanned documents, ERN range 0668 and 0649, again in the Serbian language, handwritten Cyrillic. Most importantly and crucially, we have a transcription into Latin script. And what has been transcribed from the Cyrillic to the Latin are the so-called black and white scans. There's no evidence that there was any quality control, any proper review or safe-guards put in place when someone typed the Cyrillic into Latin script. This Latin script was then translated into English and becomes the working document for this Trial Chamber. That's why the English ERN range is still the same as the black and white scan, the 0668, 0649. We say that in these circumstances it would be antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings to admit or to not exclude an English translation of a document that's gone through one version of transcription. It's like the old children's game of whispering in the ear of your neighbour and having your neighbour pass the message on. Who knows, and God only knows, what human error or other errors may have occurred in the transcription of the Cyrillic into Latin and then from the Latin -- B/C/S into English. But there's more, we say. You've heard that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you to fully under this point, if would you assist me by developing, Mr. O'Sullivan, the nature of the proceedings before this Tribunal relating as they do to events that would have occurred in a place where English is not the native language would have produced a whole host of documents which had to be translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- and transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- and transcribed, and there is a well-established procedure in the structure of the Tribunal's work for the translation of documents and for where there are disputes as to the accuracy of the translation - and I underline translation - for verification. Do I understand you to be saying that these exhibits or these intended exhibits fall outside of that -- that established procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the protocol that's followed here of transcription before translation, I'm not sure how widespread that is. But we also have two scanned versions which purport to be the same document. Or two scanning procedures of the same documents. And we say that's problematic because you will not know - and I want to go further with this - based on the evidence you've heard, you should have concern. And it's this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, I'm sorry to interrupt you again, but wouldn't the simplest way of dealing with your point be to check the translation, the English version we have in the Latin script, with the scanned version, or indeed with the original, of the notebooks at any point where there seems to be a difference in the meaning? In other words, if what is in the original corresponds -- in the original language in the B/C/S corresponds to the English version or vice versa, then there is really no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You're referring to the Cyrillic text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The original Cyrillic ends up in a Latin English translation. And these are the two extremes which we need to compare and hold together.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. So you're raising, also, the problematic issue of the intermediate transcription from B/C/S Cyrillic into B/C/S Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that part I think you could skip. In the end, it's the original Cyrillic and the final English translation in the Latin script that we need to compare. And are you able, here, to point out any major differences?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I cannot because I cannot read the Cyrillic. But the point is that the translation isn't based on the Cyrillic; the translation is based on someone having typed the Cyrillic into Latin. And that is a problem, because if you're being asked to rely on the truthfulness of the contents, you can't, and you shouldn't. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But how is that different from any other similar procedure that has been applied to a number of documents before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Because the original is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, if I were in the court, I would object strongly to it. Precisely. Why multiply the problems with human error? That's precisely the point. If that's the procedure followed, I would -- well, I'm making my submission that that ought not to be the way to proceed. And I would add that based on the testimony of this witness we see that he's found discrepancies in nine of the 18 documents he looked at. What he was purportedly shown by the Prosecution - I'm referring to P1750 - this chart, in one instance - that's document 6 on P1750 - the document he's shown is 324 pages less than what the Prosecution purported it to be. Document 9 had three more pages. Document 12 had 84 fewer pages. Document 15 had 11 fewer. Document 17 had seven more. Document 18 had 42 more. And when he comes into the court, he's not shown these documents; he's shown the colour scan. So he comes to the Tribunal in April, is asked to review 18 documents; comes in the court, he's not shown those ones; and these documents show that he looked at, apparently, in many instances, different documents. So I'm coupling this together as a situation which we say is very problematic. And where did the documents come from? Well, according to Mr. Hannis they come from Mrs. Mladic. We have no evidence surrounding the search and seizure. We have no explanation why there's been two scanned sets of documents. We have no evidence regarding the chain of custody. There's no proof, in fact, that these are the contemporaneous documents. Are these the contemporaneous documents? We saw yesterday that in reference to an entry regarding Mr. -- or person named Pecanac at page 18272, General Milovanovic says, and I quote: "It seems to me as though he," meaning Mladic, "had a premonition that those notes would eventually end up here, so he wanted to disassociate himself in advance." Well, that notebook, that notebook is from July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that notebook is from July 1992. And I would submit that I don't think General Mladic had a premonition of the ICTY months before it even was created. And the fact that we have entries that refer to public events or events that have -- have minutes attached to them like assemblies or president meetings advances nothing. If these are not the contemporaneous notes, they could be created after by the person -- by a person who is aware of these minutes. If they're sitting in a room on video, perhaps the easiest thing to do is to repeat what's said during that meeting or what's in the transcript of that meeting. So, again, we say that under Rule 95 this evidence should be excluded because the methods of and way in which it was obtained casts down on its reliability and its admission would be antithetical to a fair trial. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution wish to -- it's time for the break now, but does -- if the Prosecution wishes to reply to these submissions, I suppose we would hear them as soon as the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly disagree that there's anything about how this evidence was obtained or presented to you that rises to the level of being something that should be excluded under Rule 95. That rule talks about things where evidence is -- is recovered by torturing someone and getting a confession --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that is what I thought as well, but Mr. O'Sullivan may be correct. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I can address the other arguments if you need me, but I don't think he's made a sufficient showing. And he has known about this situation with the Latin transcription and the English translation from that from the Cyrillic original. I would suggest, if he wanted to challenge that he should have filed a motion in writing before we got here and we could have addressed it with the General. But he also had the opportunity to ask him questions about if there were any portions where he believed that there was some discrepancy between English translation and what was in the Cyrillic original; he didn't do that. And he hasn't shown you -- he hasn't pointed to you one instance where there's a problem with the translation. I think you're allowed to presume some regularity here and that you should forthwith deny his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to ask Mr. O'Sullivan whether the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and - I'm sorry - if you do have a concern about chain of custody, we have proffered a witness or two for that, if need be. And if you're going to keep out the evidence because of a lack of that evidence, we would insist that you give us the opportunity to present those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Although we're past time for the break, the last point that Mr. -- last-but-one point that Mr. Hannis made, I was going to ask Mr. O'Sullivan whether the -- there is a rule of evidence with which we would -- you and I would be familiar from our respective jurisdictions which goes under the Latin tag, omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta esse, and I'm sure it applies in some form or other in all legal systems. But I've known that rule to apply, obviously, in terms of official acts, but I would have thought that my analogy applies to something like the protocols for translation in an institution such as this. But think about it, and we'll -- we'll hear you when we come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I followed your direction over the break and thought about your suggestion on the protocol of CLSS. I realized it's the protocol. I would submit that it's an unwise protocol. And I leave it at that. And the -- I think it's been clear throughout, during our position on these documents, but just to be absolutely clear: We do object to them, and we object and oppose them being admitted for the truth of their contents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Yes, is the witness available?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, is there any ruling at this point, or are you -- with regard to the colour and black and white, are you waiting for some kind of report back from ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think we have to wait for -- the -- the -- if I can go back to where -- to your -- what you had indicated when we started today - and please correct me if I misunderstood anything you said - that you had performed the type of examination we in mind in respect of one item, which was at that point, as I understood it, only a specimen, but you would have -- you would have to complete the like exercise in respect of all of the items which have been given parallel numbers and then you would make the -- as a said, an oral submission would suffice and that would be it. But I don't -- I think it would be premature for us to go further until you would have reported or submitted - choose your word - that the -- the comparison having been done, in -- in your Chambers that the -- that the -- as to what should be admitted -- what should be marked, which version should be marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, then I guess you're content to let me do that and, in essence, report to you as an officer of the court, not has a witness, regarding that comparison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Because the -- the -- although the -- we are not unmindful of the basal objection to the Defence as to the admissibility of this material - and I come back to using the word that I chose earlier - in essence, we are satisfied that it may be admitted on the basis of the testimony of the witness who has been called who is able to identify the handwriting of -- of General Mladic. The question, the only live question that remains, is the accuracy of the two versions which for technical reasons or administrative reasons happen to be -- have been placed before the Court. And once the -- the -- and, therefore, we require you as the moving party to satisfy us as to which of these - you have a blue version, you have a black version - which of these versions you rely, because it may very well be that when you perform your examination you may find in some instances you prefer the colour version and in others the monochromatic version, but that remains to be seen. But you would recall that each of the items has been given a separate number and that allows you to make different representations in respect of each of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And from that can I take it that with regard to the submission about these documents not being admissible because of Rule 95 that you're denying that request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Concerning translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I personally would like to hear an explanation, if there is any, about the discrepancy in the page numbers. Not now, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I know the answer to some of them right off the top of my head. The others, I will have to do a little more research. But thank you for directing my attention. Because still, I don't know what your ruling is about the submission that because there's a Latin transcription of a Cyrillic original that's translated in English then the evidence is not reliable and should not be admitted. I -- I hope you are taking the position that that is denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will formally speak to that before we rise for the day, Mr. Hannis. But as far as you are concerned, we would only expect you to perform the exercise that I would have given details of, incorporating, of course, Judge Delvoie's question, and come back to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Could you kindly make the solemn declaration on the card that the usher has handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we need to go into private session for the first questions Your Honours intend to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I take it that you're hearing me in a language you understand because of your responses so far. Would you confirm that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I would, first of all, point out is that the solemn declaration that you have made imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony, and the penalty for failure to do so is that the Tribunal has the power to impose penalties for perjury under the Statutes that constitutes it. The -- you have been called by the Prosecution under an expedited procedure and -- but before I go into the time that we expect that you would be with us, I would confirm that there are certain protective measures which have been afforded to you; namely, that the ... in addition to the -- you're testifying under a pseudonym, there is also a technical procedure employed so that your face is concealed. Therefore, that -- whereas your testimony is public in the sense that persons can hear what you are saying, save for when we are in private session as we are now, they will not be able to identify you. The -- we are in the last hour of today's sitting, and we will resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon in this courtroom. The Court rises at 7.00 and sits for a portion of a day because the limited courtroom facilities have to be made available for other trials. So when we rise at 7.00 this evening, your testimony will continue when we reconvene at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. The -- you having testified previously would be familiar with the procedures of the Tribunal; therefore, I need only remind you that the side calling you, in this case the Prosecution, begins. And they have indicated that their examination of you should last for two and a half hours. The Prosecution -- sorry, the Defence of the first accused, Stanisic, has indicated two hours. And the Defence of the second accused, Zupljanin, has indicated an hour and a half. So that would take us into tomorrow, and the -- I would invite the -- while we remain in private session, I would invite Ms. Korner to begin. The only thing I would add is that the -- there are breaks in the sittings of the day, every 90 minutes, to allow for the tapes to be changed. And that facilitates the convenience of yourself and -- and everybody in and about the courtroom. And those breaks are of 20 minutes' duration. But if at any time you need to take a break, we would, of course, accommodate you. The -- before I invite Ms. Korner to begin, I would ask the usher to hand to you the pseudonym sheet which the Prosecution has. And if you're satisfied that it accurately states your name and date of birth, I would ask you to sign it and hand it back to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may use the opportunity, while the witness is signing that document, I will not take two hours. It's because of time planning and because of the OTP. Perhaps about 30 minutes only for the subjects cropped up during this examination, but I wasn't planning on asking this witness any questions after the Zupljanin Defence finishes with this witness. Just to err on the side of caution, I would like to announce 30 minutes for myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. That -- the pseudonym sheet is admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1768, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, can I deal with the timing. I think Your Honours were going back to what I originally asked for when the witness was going to be viva voce. In fact, I hope to be able to conclude my examination-in-chief within this session. And I don't believe that Mr. Krgovic is going to be anything like as long as he originally estimated. Your Honours, what I propose to do now, if we can remain in private session a little bit, is to deal with his background, then summarize the evidence he gave beforehand, which we can then go back into open session for, and then ask a few follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I think it's right - and we're still in private session -

utterances.speaker: ST-065
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The evidence that you gave was in the case of -- against Milomir Stakic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-065
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I think it's also right, as you told the Court in Stakic, that you were not, at any stage, a member of the Bosniak party, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: ST-065
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can now go into open session while I just summarize the rest of the evidence he gave, because that should not reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to summarize for the Court the evidence that you gave in the Stakic case, but the Court does in fact have the full transcript. I think it's also right you were given the opportunity yesterday to re-listen to that evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-065
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And appreciating that there's some years gone by, but if you were asked those questions again as you were asked in the Stakic case, would your answers be the same, essentially?

utterances.speaker: ST-065
utterances.text: I think they would come down to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Appreciating there's an even bigger gap of time. Now let me just, as I say, summarize that evidence. You described the attack that took place in the Brdo region on 20th of July, 1992, which included the village of Biscani. The men who carried out the attack wore various uniforms, including police uniforms. You and your father were ordered to a collection point by a cafe in the village, whilst you were there, you gave evidence that you saw armed men order two people to take away a dead body, and then those men who were ordered to take away the body were shot, and you knew all three of the people. Again, other people that you knew were beaten by the armed men. Whilst you were waiting there, a man arrived in a police car, and you recognised him and identified him as a man called Dragan Knezovic, who's now on trial at Sarajevo, and this Knezovic had a conversation with you and told you that he would return, and, as he put it, save you. Your Honours, that's at the transcript page 6865. You were taken with others, including your father, to Trnopolje in a bus which came from Autotransport Prijedor. A second bus arrived at Trnopolje after yours. Some 12 people were ordered to remain on the bus and then taken away, and you later heard that they had been killed. You remained at Trnopolje until the 21st of August. You described the layout of the camp and the conditions at the camp, including an incident where someone was cold-bloodedly killed. You told the Court in Stakic that eventually all the women and children were transported from Trnopolje to Travnik so that by the 21st of August only men were left at the camp. You said that each time a convoy came to Trnopolje it was accompanied by members of the intervention platoon from Prijedor. You described the events in detail of the 21st of August, the arrival of the buses, the intervention platoon, and one of the men who was at Trnopolje before the buses left was Dragan Knezovic. Kuruzovic, the camp commander whom you knew, was present when the buses were loaded, and your father was with you. After being joined by the other buses at the Kozarac cross-roads, you described the trip to Vlasic and how those on the buses were robbed by members of the intervention platoon during the journey. You described in detail the execution scene and the police who carried out the executions, some of whom you knew personally. One of the police involved in the killings said just before the shooting began, Here we exchange the dead for the dead and the living for the living. And you believed that that was a man called Mrdja. As you were lined up on the cliff edge, kneeling, the shooting started, and your father then pushed you over the edge. You fell, and in falling your ankle was severely broken. You crawled - and you described in detail that - on all fours for some distance over the next 24 hours until you crossed the river and you found an abandoned mill. There you were discovered by some members of the army who, in fact, as you told the Court, assisted you by bringing you a horse and taking you to a village. From there you were taken to Skender Vakuf and then to Banja Luka hospital. When your wound was finally looked at, at the hospital, it had become worm-infested. You were anaesthetised, and when you recovered consciousness, your whole leg been encased in plaster. Whilst you and other men of non-Serb extraction - nationality, I should say - were at the hospital, you were beaten. Your wound was never properly treated. It festered. And eventually, when you were moved to another hospital in Paprikovac, where you remained until October, it was discovered that there was no further treatment that was possible, and your foot and part of your leg were amputated. And during the course of this time, you were interviewed on a number of occasions, first in an ambulance on the way to Skender Vakuf, and also in Banja Luka. I appreciate, sir, that's a very shortened summary of the evidence you give. But, as I say, the Trial Chamber have your -- the transcript. Sir, I want to ask you a few follow-up questions to what you said in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we rise, I would return to the application which -- to the objection which was raised by Mr. O'Sullivan for the admission into evidence of several documents which had been identified by the Witness ST-260 and which had been marked for identification. As I understand the objections articulated by Mr. O'Sullivan, his first objection was that there had not been sufficient evidence led as to the chain of custody of the diaries on which the Prosecution -- which the Prosecution were seeking to tender. But I would remind counsel that the -- in the course of the Prosecution's case it had sought to add to its witness list an investigator who would have assisted in establishing the chain of custody of these documents, and the Chamber would have ruled that what was in issue was the authenticity of the documents and the -- inasmuch as the Witness 260 was to be called, it was wholly unnecessary to lead a witness to establish the chain of custody because how the documents came into the possession of the Prosecution was irrelevant. What was of importance was whether there were documents which the witness whom the Prosecution intended to call could speak to and could assist the Chamber. So, therefore, that aspect of Mr. O'Sullivan's objection to the admission of the documents has been -- is overruled as being encompassed within the earlier ruling of the Chamber. As to what I understand to be the summary of the second part of his objection - and I am aware that he would have laid down several planks to this, but I think that I do him no disservice when I say they could all be embraced under one head - and that is this matter of the Cyrillic original, the -- the various scanned images of the Cyrillic original, the translation of the -- sorry, the rendering of the Cyrillic original in Latin and then the transcript -- the translation of the Latin into an English version. As we would have indicated to counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis, the question of the accuracy of the scans is in the Chamber's view a purely technical matter. And having regard to the explanation that he began to give in terms of one that he was able to deal with between last evening and today, it is something which the Chamber would be content with having a report from the Prosecution as to which of the two versions -- on which they -- which they seek to put into evidence would be brought in. This is not a novel. And, indeed, it has happened on several other occasion where a document sought to be tendered there have been two versions and upon a checking it has been found that there is an more accurate version that's available, and that's all we're inviting the Prosecution to do here. As regards the other part of Mr. O'Sullivan's objection, that is, the -- what could have happened between the move from the original Cyrillic script through the Latin rendering of that to the English translation, we are of the view that the protocols which are in place in the Tribunal and which have been applied across the board to all other exhibits apply in this case, and it is -- we operate from the presumption that the translation process has been correctly and faithfully done. But, of course, that rule is a rebuttal one. And if there is a challenge to the accuracy of the translations, then the procedures are, again, well in place for that to be dealt with. We note, in passing, that the Defence did not challenge, when the witness was on the stand, the foundation of his evidence, namely, that he was able to recognise the handwriting of General Mladic from the scanned copies of the Cyrillic version that he had before him. The -- and that, of course, is qualified by the -- what I have alluded to earlier as to the versions that were in colour and the versions that were in black monochrome. So against that background, the submissions of the Defence for the Accused Stanisic in this regard are overruled, and we return to the -- we affirm the application originally made by Mr. Hannis that subject to what I would have indicated before, that the documents, once the -- once it has been -- the Chamber is satisfied as to which is the accurate versions are admissible.

ST-228, Ewan Brown, and 181; we had to call them -- it was our determination which order but we had to call them. We took that as a ruling. And indeed we came back later and said - because we -- at one stage we suggested that we might have to get a witness summons for 181 - that we didn't have to get a witness summons and he would be coming on the 10th of January. So -- which is why we got confused yesterday when Your Honours gave us a ruling on the basis that it was -- that there'd been an objection by us that it was a bit late on -- but the objection that the Defence's application was a bit late. But the objection we raised about that - which wasn't really an objection, because I was dealing with it orally - was in relation to 191. So that's why we got truly confused as to whether you were now ruling about 191 but had said 181 by mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no. It was 181.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because, I mean, in fact, if what Judge Harhoff said wasn't a ruling, then the rest -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... .

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think -- can I say, this was -- all counsel understood that you'd made a ruling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay. Well, I have the transcript here in front of me and it says: "Finally, the Chamber is minded also to allow the re-call -- to re-call ST-181." So that, in our view --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- was not a ruling, but we already anticipated on the planning for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I think, perhaps -- and can I put it this way, as politely that -- if it had been said, if we rule that you have to call him, you will have to call him in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I think that's where the confusion arose. But, of course, Your Honours, we do -- if that's possible, we do need to know about 191 - it's most unfortunate they have the same -- similar numbers - before the recess so we can get -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we will -- you will soon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we'll rule on that tomorrow, by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are reminded that it would be useful - and that's a deliberate understatement - if the parties could e-mail any issues which should be dealt with in the Status Conference by tomorrow -- oh, sorry, by Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the adjournment to 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.
